faq.q: Why does wheeze sometimes disappear in a severe attack?

faq.a: Yes; inactivated influenza vaccine reduces risk of viral‑triggered exacerbations.
faq.q: Can a patient with asthma safely receive a flu vaccine?

faq.a: At the first sign of moderate or severe exacerbation, or if the patient does not improve after 3–4 SABA doses.
faq.q: When should oral steroids be started?

exam: What is the first medication you would give to a patient with a moderate asthma exacerbation and why — SABA via spacer; rapid bronchodilation with minimal equipment.
How do you differentiate a severe asthma attack from a pneumothorax on bedside examination — absence of unilateral hyper‑resonance, presence of bilateral wheeze, and normal chest expansion.

A patient with known asthma presents with fever and productive purulent sputum; what additional investigation is indicated and why — sputum Gram stain / GeneXpert to detect bacterial infection or TB, guiding antibiotics.
Explain why high‑dose aspirin is contraindicated in acute asthma — it blocks COX‑1, increasing leukotriene production and worsening bronchospasm.
You have no peak flow meter; how do you assess severity — use clinical signs: speech ability, accessory muscle use, SpO2, and response to initial SABA.
What are the red‑flag signs that require immediate transfer to a higher‑level facility — silent chest, SpO2 <90% despite O2, altered mental status, severe tachycardia or bradycardia.
Why is a spacer preferred over a nebuliser in low‑resource settings when inhalers are available — it delivers drug efficiently with less oxygen consumption and lower cost.
After stabilising an acute attack, what step‑up therapy reduces future exacerbations and why — low‑dose inhaled corticosteroid or ICS‑LABA combination to control airway inflammation.
ai.title: Acute Asthma Exacerbation
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A sudden worsening of asthma symptoms caused by reversible airway obstruction. Recognise severity, identify triggers, and start rapid bronchodilator and anti‑inflammatory therapy, especially where resources are limited.

b: Diagnosis is clinical; spirometry (if available) shows a fall in peak expiratory flow (PEF) > 30% from personal best or > 50% from predicted.
Absence of fever, focal crackles or unilateral findings helps exclude infection or pneumothorax.
sections.p: An acute asthma exacerbation is a rapid increase in airway narrowing leading to wheeze, dyspnoea, chest tightness and cough in a patient with known asthma.

b: Mild: PEF 70‑80% predicted, able to speak in sentences, no accessory muscle use.
Moderate: PEF 40‑69% predicted, speaks in phrases, uses intercostal muscles.
Severe: PEF <40% predicted, speaks only single words, marked accessory muscle use, SpO2 <92% on room air.
Life‑threatening: Silent chest, bradycardia, exhaustion, SpO2 <90% despite oxygen.
sections.p: Severity is graded by symptoms, peak flow, and response to initial treatment.

b: Respiratory infections (viral, bacterial, TB) – most common trigger.
Air‑pollution: biomass smoke, dust, seasonal pollen.
Poor adherence to inhaled corticosteroids – often due to cost or lack of inhaler devices.
Co‑morbidities: HIV‑related lung disease, schistosomiasis‑associated airway hyper‑reactivity.
Herbal remedies or over‑the‑counter bronchodilators causing paradoxical bronchospasm.
sections.p: Identify precipitating factors; in low‑resource East African settings infections and environmental irritants dominate.

b: Rapid, shallow breathing; use of neck and intercostal muscles.
Wheezing that may become quiet (silent chest) in severe obstruction.
Cough productive of clear sputum; rarely purulent unless infection supervenes.
sections.p: Patients present with worsening wheeze, cough, chest tightness and breathlessness that may be nocturnal or triggered by a known irritant.

t.b: How much airway obstruction is present? – A fall >30% from baseline confirms exacerbation severity.
Is oxygenation adequate? – SpO2 <92% signals need for supplemental O2.
Rule out pneumonia, pneumothorax, or cardiac failure – hyperinflated lungs with flat diaphragms support asthma.
Look for eosinophilia (allergic trigger) or neutrophilia (infection). – If unavailable, treat empirically based on clinical picture.

t.a: Sputum Gram stain / GeneXpert (TB endemic areas)
t.b: Detect bacterial infection or TB when fever, productive purulent sputum, or weight loss present – guides antibiotic choice.

b: Silent chest, inability to speak, bradycardia, altered mental status.
Rapid rise in CO2 (if capnography available) or worsening hypercapnia.
Pneumothorax after vigorous forced expirations.
Superimposed pneumonia or pulmonary embolism.
sections.p: Recognise features that herald impending respiratory failure or secondary disease.

b: High‑flow oxygen to keep SpO2 ≥94% (target 92‑96% in COPD co‑morbidity).
Short‑acting β2‑agonist (SABA) via metered‑dose inhaler with spacer – first‑line bronchodilator; avoid nebuliser if oxygen supply limited.
Ipratropium bromide (if available) added to SABA for moderate‑severe attacks – anticholinergic bronchodilation.
If no inhaler devices, use nebulised salbutamol with oxygen‑conserving circuit; monitor for tachycardia.
Treat identified infection (e.g., amoxicillin for bacterial pneumonia, anti‑TB therapy if GeneXpert positive).
Avoid non‑selective β‑blockers, high‑dose aspirin, and sedatives that may worsen bronchospasm.
sections.p: Treat the trigger, reverse bronchoconstriction, and control inflammation while monitoring for deterioration.

b: Review inhaler technique; provide spacer if not already used.
Step‑up controller therapy: low‑dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) or combination ICS‑LABA.
Identify and mitigate triggers – indoor smoke, mold, seasonal pollen.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus; screen for HIV and treat if positive.
Arrange follow‑up within 1‑2 weeks to assess control and adjust regimen.
sections.p: After acute control, optimise long‑term asthma management to prevent recurrence.

b: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease – usually older smokers, less reversibility.
Bronchiolitis in infants – viral prodrome, no prior asthma history.
Heart failure – crackles, peripheral oedema, cardiomegaly on X‑ray.
Pulmonary embolism – sudden pleuritic pain, tachycardia, normal wheeze.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic wheeze or dyspnoea.

b: Normal PEF in a patient using a poorly fitting spacer – may underestimate severity.
Chest X‑ray may appear normal early in severe asthma; rely on clinical signs.
Eosinophil count can be low during viral infection despite allergic asthma.

whenToSeekHelp: Silent chest or inability to speak
Severe tachycardia >130 bpm or bradycardia <50 bpm
